title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
summary: Electrostatic potential, potential due to a point charge and a dipole, equipotential surfaces, potential energy, conductors and dielectrics, capacitors, their combinations and stored energy.
source: Sample content written for demonstration by AR Group Ventures editorial team. Not an official BSEB question.

notes.text: The electrostatic potential at a point is the work done by an external agent in bringing a unit positive test charge from infinity to that point, without acceleration. It is a scalar quantity. SI unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹. The potential difference between two points is the work done per unit charge in moving a test charge from one point to the other.

notes.label: Potential due to a point charge
notes.text: V = (1/4πε₀) · (q / r),   and for a dipole at distance r (r ≫ a):  V = (1/4πε₀) · (p cos θ / r²)

items: Potential due to a group of charges is the algebraic sum of the potentials due to each charge (superposition).
Relation between field and potential: E = −dV/dr. The field points in the direction in which potential falls fastest.
An equipotential surface is one on which the potential is the same at every point. For a point charge these are concentric spheres; for a uniform field they are parallel planes perpendicular to E.
Equipotential surfaces never cut each other, and the electric field is always perpendicular to them.

notes.text: Potential is a scalar, so it can be added directly without worrying about direction. No work is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface, since the potential difference is zero. On the axis of a dipole V is maximum; on the equatorial line V = 0.

notes.label: Electrostatic potential energy
notes.text: U = (1/4πε₀) · (q₁q₂ / r)  for two charges;   U = −pE cos θ = −p · E  for a dipole in a uniform field

items: Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium E = 0, all excess charge resides on the outer surface, and the whole conductor is an equipotential.
Just outside the surface of a charged conductor E = σ/ε₀, perpendicular to the surface. A cavity inside a conductor has zero field (electrostatic shielding).

A dielectric is an insulator. In an external field its molecules acquire induced dipole moments (polarisation), which produce an opposing field and reduce the net field inside by a factor K, the dielectric constant (K = ε/ε₀ > 1).

notes.label: Parallel plate capacitor
notes.text: C = Q/V;   C = ε₀A / d  (air between plates);   C = Kε₀A / d  (dielectric fills the gap);   SI unit: farad (F)

notes.label: Combination of capacitors and stored energy
notes.text: Series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + …;   Parallel: C = C₁ + C₂ + …;   U = ½CV² = Q²/2C = ½QV

The farad is a very large unit; practical capacitors are measured in μF (10⁻⁶ F), nF (10⁻⁹ F) and pF (10⁻¹² F). Inserting a dielectric of constant K increases the capacitance K times. Energy stored per unit volume in the field (energy density) is ½ε₀E². In series the charge on every capacitor is the same; in parallel the voltage across each is the same.

objective.question: The SI unit of electrostatic potential is:
objective.explanation: Potential is work done per unit charge, so its unit is joule per coulomb, which is called the volt (V).
objective.source: Sample content written for demonstration by AR Group Ventures editorial team. Not an official BSEB question.

objective.question: The work done in moving a charge from one point to another on an equipotential surface is:
objective.explanation: Every point on an equipotential surface is at the same potential, so the potential difference is zero and W = q × ΔV = 0.
objective.source: Sample content written for demonstration by AR Group Ventures editorial team. Not an official BSEB question.

objective.question: The correct relation between electric field E and potential V is:
objective.explanation: The electric field is the negative gradient of the potential: E = −dV/dr. The minus sign shows that the field points in the direction of decreasing potential.

objective.question: A parallel plate capacitor has capacitance C with air between its plates. When the gap is completely filled with a dielectric of dielectric constant K, the capacitance becomes:
objective.explanation: With a dielectric, C' = Kε₀A/d = K × (ε₀A/d) = KC, so the capacitance increases K times.

objective.question: The electric field inside a charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is:
options: equal to the field at the surface
objective.explanation: If there were a field inside, free electrons would move and the conductor would not be in equilibrium. Hence E = 0 inside and the excess charge stays on the surface.
objective.source: Sample content written for demonstration by AR Group Ventures editorial team. Not an official BSEB question.

objective.question: The potential energy of an electric dipole of moment p placed parallel to a uniform electric field E (θ = 0°) is:
objective.explanation: U = −pE cos θ. At θ = 0°, cos θ = 1, so U = −pE, the minimum value, which is the position of stable equilibrium.
objective.source: Sample content written for demonstration by AR Group Ventures editorial team. Not an official BSEB question.

objective.question: Two capacitors of 4 μF and 6 μF are connected in parallel. The equivalent capacitance is:
objective.explanation: In parallel the capacitances simply add: C = 4 + 6 = 10 μF.
objective.source: Sample content written for demonstration by AR Group Ventures editorial team. Not an official BSEB question.

important.question: Define electrostatic potential at a point. Write its SI unit and state whether it is a scalar or a vector quantity.
answerOutline: Electrostatic potential at a point is the work done by an external agent in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point without acceleration: V = W/q₀.
SI unit: volt (V); 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
It is a scalar quantity, because work and charge are both scalars.
For a point charge q, V = (1/4πε₀) · q/r, and the potential at infinity is taken as zero.
important.source: Sample content written for demonstration by AR Group Ventures editorial team. Not an official BSEB question.

important.question: What is an equipotential surface? Why can two equipotential surfaces never intersect each other?
answerOutline: An equipotential surface is a surface on which every point has the same electrostatic potential.
Examples: concentric spheres around a point charge; parallel planes perpendicular to a uniform field.
If two such surfaces intersected, the point of intersection would have two different potentials at the same time, which is impossible.
Also, the field must be perpendicular to an equipotential surface; at an intersection the field would have two directions, which cannot happen.
important.source: Sample content written for demonstration by AR Group Ventures editorial team. Not an official BSEB question.

important.question: Derive the expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor. How does the capacitance change when a dielectric slab completely fills the space between the plates?
answerOutline: Consider two parallel metal plates each of area A separated by a small distance d, carrying charges +Q and −Q. Surface charge density σ = Q/A.
Using Gauss's law, the field between the plates is uniform: E = σ/ε₀ = Q/(ε₀A); outside the plates the fields of the two sheets cancel.
Potential difference between the plates V = E × d = Qd/(ε₀A).
Capacitance C = Q/V = ε₀A/d.
C is directly proportional to the plate area and inversely proportional to the separation; it does not depend on Q or V.
When a dielectric of dielectric constant K fills the gap, the field reduces to E/K, so V reduces to V/K and the capacitance becomes C' = Kε₀A/d = KC, i.e. it increases K times.
important.source: Sample content written for demonstration by AR Group Ventures editorial team. Not an official BSEB question.

important.question: Derive the expression for the energy stored in a charged capacitor. Also obtain the expression for the equivalent capacitance of three capacitors connected in series.
answerOutline: Energy stored: at an instant when the charge on the capacitor is q, its potential is V = q/C. Work done to add a further charge dq is dW = V dq = (q/C) dq.
Total work to charge it from 0 to Q: W = ∫₀^Q (q/C) dq = Q²/2C. This work is stored as electrostatic energy, U = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV.
Series combination: capacitors C₁, C₂, C₃ connected end to end across a battery of voltage V carry the same charge Q on each.
Potential differences across them are V₁ = Q/C₁, V₂ = Q/C₂, V₃ = Q/C₃, and V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃.
If C is the equivalent capacitance, V = Q/C, so Q/C = Q/C₁ + Q/C₂ + Q/C₃, giving 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + 1/C₃.
The equivalent capacitance in series is smaller than the smallest individual capacitance.
important.source: Sample content written for demonstration by AR Group Ventures editorial team. Not an official BSEB question.
